newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget pact seeks balance beyond 2002.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget pact seeks balance beyond 2002.

text.p: The agreement reached between President Clinton and the Republican-led Congress is designed to reach a balanced budget by 2002 and hopes for surplus thereafter, according to documents released by the congressional leadership.

The plan includes an $85 billion net tax cut over five years. While not specifying tax details the statement said the pact would "accomodate a child tax credit, death tax relief, capital gains tax relief," as well as expand individual retirement accounts and offer some tax breaks for college costs.
The leadership said the pact "saves Medicare for ten years" through reforms of the program that will slow its growth by $115 billion over the next five years.
The pact includes $600 billion to $700 billion of savings in entitlement programs, which are domestic benefit programs whose spending is manadatory.

"As important as this plan is, it is only the beginning," the leadership statement said. "A lot of work is needed to implement this plan and to keep it intact. But there is a firm commitment now on both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue (White House and Congress) to do so," it said.
The statement added that the budget pact provides funds for domestic priorities of transportation, housing and education.
